article.title: Air Force Major Jason Watson Remains Jailed After Calling for Trump’s Impeachment
article.intro: Jason Watson faces military charges over his public criticism of Donald Trump. His attorney reports solitary confinement as the military prosecution continues.
article.body:
U.S. Air Force Maj. Jason P. Watson remains in pretrial confinement amid a military prosecution over his public criticism of President Donald Trump. His attorney, Christopher Mutimer, says the officer is being held alone around the clock.

In remarks broadcast by CNN on October 10, Mutimer said Watson was in “solitary confinement 24 hours a day,” including when eating or exercising. That account is attributed to his lawyer; NPPC has not independently verified his daily detention conditions.

From the Capitol protest to military confinement

Watson drew national attention on July 1, 2026, when he stood in uniform on the U.S. Capitol steps holding a sign demanding impeachment, conviction and removal. He had spoken at a news conference calling for Trump and Vice President JD Vance to leave office. Capitol Police arrested him, and the Air Force subsequently restricted him to Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling while investigating his conduct.

The July arrest and the later period of pretrial confinement are distinct. CNN reported that the Air Force ordered Watson into pretrial confinement on August 18, the day after he again criticized Trump in a television interview. August reporting placed him in a Maryland county facility on a military hold. This article does not identify that facility as his verified current location.

Ten specifications under military law

According to a charging document reviewed by CNN, prosecutors preferred charges on August 24 containing ten specifications:

  • Three under Article 88, alleging contempt toward officials.
  • Five under Article 92, alleging failures to obey orders or regulations.
  • Two under Article 133, alleging conduct unbecoming an officer.

The allegations concern his remarks and interviews as well as military orders governing conduct, travel and uniforms. The Air Force confirmed the charges and said he remained entitled to due process and the presumption of innocence.

Article 88 prohibits commissioned officers from using “contemptuous words” against specified civilian officials, including the president. Watson’s defense argues that criticism on matters of public concern should not be treated as criminal contempt.

A recommendation is not a verdict

Watson appeared at an Article 32 preliminary hearing at Anacostia-Bolling on September 18. Stars and Stripes reported that he described his actions as an effort to uphold his constitutional oath. Government counsel disputed that he was being singled out and denied that the charges resulted from political pressure.

In a September 29 statement, Monument Legal, the firm representing Watson, said the preliminary hearing officer recommended dismissing allegations of prohibited partisan political activity for lack of probable cause. The defense described the report as controlled unclassified information, restricting its public release.

Those recommendations do not themselves dismiss charges or establish guilt. A convening authority decides whether and how the case proceeds. The defense has requested a special court-martial, a less severe forum than a general court-martial. Military Times reported that counsel compared Watson’s treatment with that of Marine Lt. Col. Stuart Scheller, whose criticism of military leaders over the Afghanistan withdrawal led to a special court-martial in 2021.

Confinement before conviction

Military law also sets limits on pretrial treatment. Article 13 prohibits punishment before trial and restricts confinement that is more rigorous than the circumstances require. Whether Watson’s particular conditions violate those protections has not been established in the sources reviewed for this report.

No conviction, sentence or final court-martial referral is confirmed in the material reviewed here. The charges remain allegations.

Read Jason Watson’s NPPC prisoner profile for his documented custody timeline. His supporters have organized a personal legal-defense fund through the Major Jason Watson Legal Trust.

Published October 13, 2026. This report is based on published reporting, public statements by counsel and the text of the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
